'''Chigo''' (稚児) has, broadly, the following meanings:
* In its original sense, "chigo" refers to infants and toddlers (i.e., {{ill|Infant|af|Baba|ar|رضيع|ary|مومو|ast|Ñácaru|ay|Wawa|az|Körpə|azb|کؤرپه|bar|Buzal|bcl|Umboy|be|Немаўля|be_x_old|Немаўля|bg|Бебе|bn|বাচ্চা|br|Babig|ca|Nadó|cdo|Niè-giāng-giāng|ckb|ساوا|crh|Bebiy|cs|Kojenec|cv|Нараста|cy|Babi|da|Baby|de|Säugling|diq|Pıt|el|Βρέφος|eo|Bebo|es|Bebé|et|Imik|eu|Haurtxo|fa|نوزاد|fi|Vauvaikä|fr|Nourrisson|fy|Poppe|ga|Naíonán|gan|毛伢子|gcr|Bébé|gd|Naoidhean|gl|Bebé|gn|Mitãra'y|ha|Jariri|hak|Ô-nga-é|he|ינקות|hi|शिशु|hr|Dojenče|ht|Bebe|hu|Csecsemő|hy|Կրծքի երեխա|iba|Anak mit|id|Bayi|io|Bebeo|it|Bebè|iu|ᓄᑕᒐᒃ|ja|赤ちゃん|jv|Bayi|kab|Asegmi|kk|Нәресте|kn|ಶಿಶು|ko|아기|ku|Pitik|kus|Bilia|ky|Наристе балдар|la|Infans|lb|Puppelchen|lmo|Bambin|lt|Kūdikystė|lv|Zīdainis|mg|Zazakely|ml|ശിശു|mr|अर्भकावस्था|ms|Bayi|mzn|زلغ|ne|शिशु|new|ह्यांगु मचा|nl|Baby|nn|Spedbarn|no|Spedbarn|pa|ਨਿੱਕਾ ਬਾਲ|pdc|Bobbeli|pl|Niemowlę|pt|Bebé|qu|Pallpa|ro|Sugar|ru|Младенец|scn|Lattanti|sd|شيرخوار|sh|Dojenče|si|ළදරුවා|simple|Baby|sk|Dojča|sl|Dojenček|sn|Mucheche|so|Ilmo|sq|Foshnja|sr|Новорођенче|su|Orok|sv|Spädbarn|szy|lutungay|ta|குழந்தை|te|శిశువు|th|ทารก|tk|Bäbek|tl|Sanggol|tr|Bebek|ts|Ricece|uk|Немовля|ur|نوزائیدہ|uz|Goʻdak|vi|Trẻ sơ sinh|war|Minasus-án|wuu|小毛头|yi|עופעלע|yo|Ìkókó|zh|嬰兒|zh_min_nan|Âng-eⁿ-á|zh_yue|孲𤘅子|qid=Q998}} and {{ill|Toddler|ar|طفل متهاد|bs|Mališan|cs|Batole|de|Kleinkind|eo|Infaneto|fa|کودک نوپا|he|פעוט|hy|Վաղ հասակ|id|Balita|ja|幼児|mr|शिशुवय|nl|Peuter|no|Småbarn|pl|Okres poniemowlęcy|ru|Ранний возраст|scn|Nutricu|simple|Toddler|sq|Fëmijëria e hershme|sr|Малишан|sv|Koltålder|tr|Yeni yürüyen|uk|Малюк|zh|学步期|qid=Q1340307|lt=Toddler}}). It is thought to be a contraction of the term “chinomigo.” Later, the meaning was expanded to include young children up to around 6 years old (prior to wearing {{ill|hakamagi|ja|袴着|qid=Q30924452}} or having their hair tied). Boys and girls between the time they begin wearing hakama and untied hair up until their {{ill|Genpuku|el|Γκενπούκου|fa|گنپوکو|fr|Genpuku|id|Genbuku|it|Genpuku|ja|元服|ko|원복 (일본)|pl|Genpuku|ru|Гэмпуку|simple|Genpuku|th|เก็มปูกุ|zh|日本元服礼|qid=Q138321}} (coming-of-age ceremony) or when they start wearing {{ill|mogi|ja|裳着|pl|Mogi|qid=Q11626854}} were called {{nihongo|waraba|わらは・わらべ}}.
* In large temples, "chigo" refers to young acolytes—see section [[#Chigo in Large Temples|Chigo in Large Temples]] below.
*** By extension, the term came to denote young men who were objects of {{ill|male love|ja|男色|nl|Nanshoku|qid=Q122663390}}.
* In festivals, "chigo" refers to child participants—see section [[#Chigo in Festivals|Chigo in Festivals]] below.
* Under the "Gōchū" system of the {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ar|مقاطعة ساتسوما|de|Satsuma (Han)|es|Dominio de Satsuma|fa|قلمرو ساتسوما|fi|Satsuman daimiokunta|fr|Domaine de Satsuma|he|סצומה|id|Domain Satsuma|it|Dominio di Satsuma|ja|薩摩藩|ko|사쓰마번|ms|Domain Satsuma|nl|Satsuma (han)|pl|Satsuma (domena feudalna)|pt|Domínio de Satsuma|ru|Сацума (княжество)|sr|Сацума (феудална област)|th|แคว้นศักดินาซัตสึมะ|tl|Dominyo ng Satsuma|tr|Satsuma (beylik)|uk|Сацума-хан|vi|Phiên Satsuma|wuu|萨摩藩|zh|薩摩藩|zh_min_nan|Satuma-hoan|zh_yue|薩摩藩|qid=Q676187|lt=Satsuma Domain}}, the term denotes the younger age group. In this system, children aged approximately 6–7 to 10 are classified as {{nihongo|kochigo|こちご}}<ref group="Notes">In some regions they were also called {{nihongo|warabe|わらべ}} chigo, Hego {{nihongo|yama|やま}} chigo, or Hego chigo.</ref>, and those aged 11 to 14 or 15 are classified as {{nihongo|osechigo|おせちご}}<ref>{{Cite web|和書|url=https://blogs.mbc.co.jp/rekishi-no-chikara/583|title=郷中教育２８|date=2018-04-25|website=南日本放送|work=薩摩の教え|publisher=南日本放送|accessdate=2021-03-08}}</ref><ref group="Notes">This is the standard age division; it may vary by region.</ref>.
== Chigo in Large Temples ==
[[File:Yoshitoshi Sojobo Instructs Yoshitsune in the Sword.jpg|thumb|200px|{{ill|karasu tengu|de|Karasu Tengu|es|Karasu Tengu|ja|烏天狗|ko|가라스텐구|sv|Karasutengu|zh|烏天狗|qid=Q863869}} and {{ill|Ushiwakamaru|ja|牛若丸}} (Chigo at Kurama-dera)]]
From around the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, in large temples of the {{ill|Shingon Buddhism|en|Shingon Buddhism|qid=Q550182|lt=Shingon sect}} and the {{ill|Tiantai|en|Tiantai|qid=Q668188|lt=Tendai sect}}, a group of young trainee monks (approximately 12–18 years old) who did not shave began to appear, and these too came to be known as chigo. In such temple settings, children of royalty and high nobility were entrusted as etiquette apprentices (called "upper chigo"), those noted for their intelligence were employed as attendants (called "middle chigo"), and those with promising artistic talent (or who were sold by corrupt monks) were called "lower chigo." In the context of {{ill|Zen|en|Zen|qid=Q7953|lt=Zen Buddhism}}, this group was known as {{ill|Kasshoku|ja|喝食|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kasshoku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11419277}}.
Their hairstyles were either {{ill|tairyō|ja|垂髪}} or the {{ill|chigo mage|ja|稚児髷|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/chigo mage|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11596298}}, and they wore makeup similar to that of {{ill|Heian aristocracy|ja|平安貴族|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Heian aristocratic|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11482408}} women (sometimes including {{ill|Ohaguro|en|Ohaguro|qid=Q2016382|lt=Ohaguro}}), and donned brightly colored garments known as {{ill|Suikan|en|Suikan|qid=Q11548540|lt=Suikan}}. They sometimes also cross-dressed, making it difficult to distinguish them from girls.
Since the large temples of the Shingon and Tendai sects, which served as training grounds, were located in mountainous areas and were restricted to men ({{ill|Nyonin Kinsei|en|Nyonin Kinsei|qid=Q11446290|lt=Nyonin Kinsei}}), such chigo came to be seen as "feminine figures in a male society" and were frequently the objects of {{ill|Nanshoku|ja|男色|nl|Nanshoku|qid=Q122663390}} (although the upper chigo were generally excluded). From the medieval period onward, even in Zen temple complexes ({{ill|Zenrin|ja|禅林|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zenrin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11591187}}) and in the {{ill|Huayan|en|Huayan|qid=Q1198075|lt=Kegon sect}}, chigo and those known as kasshoku were primarily objects of male love, shūdō, and shonen-ai.
In particular, in the Tendai sect a ritual known as "Chigo Kanzō" was performed, during which the chigo were given names ending in "maru." Those who received such names were equated with {{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|Avalokiteśvara|qid=Q193849|lt=Kannon Bodhisattva}} and revered as sacred. For instance, in the {{ill|Huayan|en|Huayan|qid=Q1198075|lt=Kegon sect}} at {{ill|Tōdai-ji|en|Tōdai-ji|qid=Q460367|lt=Tōdai-ji}}, there existed a monk who maintained relationships with approximately 100 chigo.
== Chigo in Festivals ==
[[File:Chigo001.jpg|thumb|[[Fukagawa Shinmeigu]]'s chigo procession (in [[:en:Kōtō Ward|Kōtō Ward]], Tokyo)]]
(In modern usage, "chigo" in festivals generally includes children (including pre-schoolers) who participate in festivals.)
In contemporary festivals, young boys and girls (generally those below elementary school age) who wear distinctive makeup (often heavy makeup) and uniform or prescribed costumes are commonly referred to as chigo. However, whether they are called chigo depends on the festival organizers; for example, at the annual festival of {{ill|Tsurugaoka Hachimangū|en|Tsurugaoka Hachimangū|qid=Q701403|lt=Tsurugaoka Hachimangu}}, the children in the "Yaotome" or "Dōji" category may not be called chigo, whereas in festivals like the {{ill|Himeji Yukata Matsuri|ja|姫路ゆかたまつり|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Himeji Yukata Matsuri|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11447453}}, even those appearing in plain yukata (without {{ill|Hakama|en|Hakama|qid=Q164668|lt=hakama}}) may be referred to as chigo.
== Costumes and Makeup ==
[[File:Chigo Costumes in Japan (1914-09 by Elstner Hilton).jpg|thumb|200px|Chigo from the Taishō period (circa 1914)]]
The costumes of chigo are generally based on {{ill|Heian shōzoku|ja|平安装束|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Heian period attire|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11482407}} (such as {{ill|Heian shōzoku|ja|神官装束|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinkansho|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 平安装束|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11482407}} or {{ill|Miko clothing|en|Miko clothing|qid=Q17231335|lt=Miko attire}}), or a greatly simplified version thereof; {{ill|Hakama|en|Hakama|qid=Q164668|lt=hakama}} are considered indispensable. Boys often wear {{ill|eboshi|ja|烏帽子}}, while girls typically wear {{ill|tengan|ja|天冠}}. Common accessories include fans (舞扇) and artificial flowers representing lotus, cherry blossoms, autumn leaves, etc.
The makeup typically consists of a pattern on the forehead, known as {{ill|Kōjin|ja|アヤツコ|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ayatsuko|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 荒神|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q6455190}}, or a round mark called "Kuraihoshi" (both applied in black or red), with the nasal bridge painted white. Beyond this, the makeup may be minimal (only lipstick applied) or, alternatively, as elaborate as adult formal makeup, stage makeup similar to that used in {{ill|Shosagoto|en|Shosagoto|qid=Q11545264|lt=kabuki dance}}, or even Western-style heavy makeup reminiscent of ballet. These costumes and makeup are not merely decorative; they are imbued with meanings of divinity, sacredness, and mystery, and serve as a rite of passage.
== Classification by Type ==
In festivals, chigo can be broadly classified into three types:
* Yorimashi Type
* Dance/Performing Arts Type
* Procession Type
=== Yorimashi Type ===
From ancient times, it was believed that divine spirits were more likely to descend upon very young children (under 6 years old). Thus, in shrine festivals, chigo who serve as "yorimashi" (physical vessels for the divine) appear. Today, they are treated as symbols of the festival; in most cases, they are boys, and usually only one, or at most three, are chosen.
=== Dance/Performing Arts Type ===
Young boys and girls who perform dances such as {{ill|Kagura|en|Kagura|qid=Q1348260|lt=Kagura}}, traditional dance (舞楽), ennen, dengaku, and fuuryū, are often referred to as chigo. In the case of miko kagura, the miko wearing miko costumes may be called chigo, and those who perform as "norizu" on the taiko stage are sometimes also considered chigo.
This type includes chigo who follow the tradition of the male trainee monks mentioned earlier.
=== Procession Type ===
This is the most commonly observed type. Chigo in this category appear during temple flower festivals (such as birth celebrations, kanbutsu-e, and Shaka’s birthday), on days commemorating the death of a deity (such as the {{ill|Oeshiki|ja|お会式|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Okaishiki|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q4328808}}), and during occasional grand ceremonies such as the large-scale Buddhist festival ({{ill|dharma assembly|ja|大法会|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Daibōkai|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 法会|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11555016}}) held once every few decades or centuries, as well as in processions at shrine festivals. In large-scale festivals, it is not uncommon for more than 200 children to appear.
In addition, children's performance of {{ill|Tegomai|ja|手古舞|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tegomai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11496936}} may also be referred to as chigo.
There is also an urban legend that if a child appears in a procession three times, they will be blessed with good fortune.
